client: I've been really stressed out lately about my grades, especially after I got a C in calculus last semester. It's like this constant weight on my chest because I feel like I've already ruined my GPA and I can't stop thinking about it. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to fix anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It sounds like this worry about your grades has really been weighing on you, and that feeling of things being "already ruined" can make it hard to see a way forward. I also notice you mentioned some doubt about whether talking will even help — and I think that's worth honoring, because it takes courage to show up anyway. What would it mean for you if we could start to loosen that weight, even just a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, I guess it would mean I could actually focus in my other classes without this constant dread hanging over me. But I keep coming back to the fact that the damage is already done — like, a C is on my transcript forever, and I don't know how loosening the weight changes that reality. I want to believe it could help, but part of me feels like feeling better about it would just be... pretending it's not a big deal when it actually is.
therapist: You're touching on something really important — there's a difference between *accepting* something and *dismissing* it, and it sounds like part of you is worried that feeling better would mean pretending the C doesn't matter, when it clearly does to you. But what if working through this isn't about minimizing the grade, but about challenging the story that one grade has permanently defined your path? I'm curious — when you imagine a future version of yourself looking back, do you think this C will carry the same weight it does right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I want to say no, that future me probably won't care as much, but right now that feels really hard to believe. Like, I know logically that one grade isn't everything, but then I start thinking about grad school or job applications and I spiral into imagining someone rejecting me specifically because of that C. It's like my brain won't let me hold onto the rational perspective for more than a few seconds before the anxiety pulls me back.
therapist: What you're describing — that tug-of-war between the logical part of you and the anxious part — is really common, and it actually has a name in CBT: it's like your rational mind and your threat-detecting mind are fighting for the mic. It's worth noticing that you *can* access that calmer perspective, even if anxiety keeps interrupting it — that's actually something we can work with and strengthen over time. Can you tell me more about what that spiral looks like — like, where does your mind usually go first when the anxiety takes over?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Usually it starts with something small, like seeing someone else's grade or a professor mentioning grad school requirements, and then my brain just jumps straight to "you're already behind and you'll never catch up." From there it snowballs into this whole narrative where I'm the person who couldn't handle college, and somehow everyone around me is doing fine while I'm falling apart. It's embarrassing to even say out loud because I know it sounds dramatic, but in the moment it feels completely real and inevitable.
therapist: Thank you for trusting me with that — and I want to gently push back on the word "dramatic," because what you're describing is a really painful thought pattern, not an overreaction. It's interesting that even as you shared something that clearly feels so heavy, there was something almost careful in the way you said it — like you were bracing for judgment, maybe even from yourself. What do you think it would feel like to describe that spiral without apologizing for it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That's a weird question to sit with, because my first instinct is to say it would feel selfish or self-indulgent, like I'm making too big a deal out of something I should just handle on my own. I think part of why I downplay it is because I'm worried that if I fully own how bad it feels, it makes it more real and harder to ignore. And honestly, I'm also scared that if I stop apologizing for it, you might actually see how much this is affecting me and think less of me for not having it together.
therapist: What you just shared takes real courage, and I want you to hear this clearly: the fact that you're struggling doesn't make me think less of you — it makes you human. I also notice you said all of that very quickly, like maybe part of you wanted to get it out before you could take it back, which makes me wonder if there's some relief in having said it. What's it like to have that fear — of being truly seen — actually out in the open now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: It's strange because there is a tiny bit of relief, but it's immediately followed by this urge to backtrack and say "but I'm probably overreacting" or "it's really not that bad." I think being seen is something I want but also kind of terrifies me, because if you really see how much a single grade has unraveled me, it confirms this fear that I'm fundamentally not cut out for this. It's like the relief and the dread are happening at the exact same time.
therapist: The way you just described that — relief and dread at the same time — is actually a really profound moment of self-awareness, and I don't want to rush past it. I'm also noticing something gentle in how you said all of this, almost quiet, like you're holding it carefully rather than letting yourself fully feel the weight of it yet. I wonder if that "fundamentally not cut out for this" fear is one we could look at more closely — because that's a very big conclusion to draw from a single grade, and I'm curious where that belief started.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think that belief has been around for a lot longer than this calculus grade, honestly. Growing up, I always felt like I had to prove I was smart enough to belong, and any mistake felt like evidence that I'd been faking it the whole time. So when I got that C, it wasn't just a grade — it felt like the moment the truth finally caught up with me.
therapist: What you just named — that the C felt like a confirmation of something you've feared about yourself for a long time — that's a really significant insight, and it reframes so much of what you've been carrying. This isn't really about calculus at all, is it; it's about a much older story that's been quietly running in the background, waiting for "proof." I'd love to explore that with you — where do you think that belief that you had to *earn* your belonging first took root?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think it probably started with my family, where academic achievement was kind of the main way you got praised or noticed. My parents weren't mean about it, but looking back, the warmth and attention always seemed to show up more when I brought home good grades, and I internalized that pretty early. I'm a little hesitant to go too deep into that right now though, because it feels like a big door to open and I'm not sure I'm ready to connect all of this back to my childhood when I came in here just wanting to feel less stressed about a grade.
therapist: Your hesitation makes complete sense, and I want you to know you're always in the driver's seat here — we don't have to go anywhere you're not ready to go. And you're right that you came in wanting relief from stress about a grade, which is completely valid; it's just that *you* were the one who started connecting the dots, and that tells me something about your own readiness, even if it feels scary. We can absolutely stay closer to the surface for now — what would feel most useful to focus on today?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think what would feel most useful is figuring out how to get through the rest of this semester without the anxiety about that C constantly derailing me when I'm trying to study or sit in class. Like, practically speaking, I still have to show up every day and function, and right now that feels really hard when part of my brain is always whispering that it's already too late. I guess I want some kind of tool or strategy, but I'm also a little skeptical that anything will actually quiet that voice down.
therapist: That's a really grounded and honest place to land — wanting practical tools while also holding some skepticism about whether they'll work, and both of those things can be true at once. One place we could start is learning to recognize and interrupt that "it's already too late" thought in the moment, because right now it's running on autopilot, but with practice you can learn to catch it before it snowballs into the full spiral. Would it help to look at what that voice is actually saying and start to build some specific responses you can use when it shows up during class or studying?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I'm open to trying that, but my worry is that in the moment when the anxiety hits, I'm so deep in it that I don't think I'll have the presence of mind to stop and use some kind of response. It's like when I'm sitting in class and that voice starts up, it doesn't feel like a thought I can argue with — it feels like the truth. How do you actually get your brain to pause long enough to even try a different response when it's convinced it already knows what's real?
therapist: You're naming one of the hardest parts of anxiety — that it doesn't announce itself as a thought, it disguises itself as reality, which makes it really difficult to create any distance from it in the moment. The good news is that the goal isn't to out-argue the voice right away; it's actually just to create a tiny crack of awareness, something as simple as noticing "there's that thought again" rather than immediately trying to defeat it. That small shift — from *being inside* the thought to *observing* it — is actually the first step, and it gets easier with practice; would you be willing to try noticing it this week without pressuring yourself to fix it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
